opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to figure out what you actually care about. A PhD is five or six years of your life, often during a period when you have the most energy and the most freedom, so it's worth spending it on a problem you genuinely find exciting, not just something that looks good on paper or that happens to be trendy at the moment.

For me, I've always loved building things. Computer graphics was the field where I could write code and immediately see something beautiful on the screen, like smoke, water, or elastic objects. That feedback loop kept me going through the hard parts. So I'd say prioritize a direction where your curiosity naturally pulls you, because research is full of failures, and intrinsic motivation is what gets you through them.

The second thing is impact over quantity. It's easy to get caught up counting papers, but in the long run people remember maybe one or two things you did. I'd rather spend a long time on something that really changes how people work, like building a tool that thousands of others can use, than publish many incremental papers. When I worked on Taichi, a lot of it wasn't the kind of thing that immediately turns into a paper, but I felt it could make high-performance computing much more accessible, and that turned out to matter a lot.

Third, take care of yourself and build good habits. Learn to manage your time, keep your health, and find people you enjoy working with. Your advisor and your collaborators make a huge difference. A PhD is a marathon, not a sprint.

And finally, don't be afraid to take some risks. A PhD is one of the few times in life where failing is relatively cheap. If you have a bold idea, try it. The worst case is you learn a lot.

r001.rationale: It advises first identifying what genuinely excites you and spending the PhD years on that kind of problem, rather than choosing work just because it looks good or is trendy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the first thing is to be honest with yourself about why you're doing it. A PhD is five or six years of your life, and if the reason is "I didn't know what else to do" or "my parents think it sounds good," that's going to be a very hard five years. The people who do well are usually the ones who have some problem they genuinely can't stop thinking about.

Second, I'd prioritize finding the right advisor over finding the most famous lab. When I was at MIT, the thing that mattered most wasn't the ranking, it was whether my advisor gave me room to go after weird ideas. Taichi started as something that didn't fit neatly into any existing agenda. If I'd been in a group where I had to produce incremental papers every quarter, it probably wouldn't have happened. So talk to the current students. Ask them how often they meet their advisor, whether they feel supported, whether they're allowed to fail.

Third, build things, not just papers. Papers are the currency of academia, I understand that, but a paper that nobody uses disappears in two years. A piece of software that people actually run teaches you things no reviewer will ever tell you. You learn what users really need, you learn engineering discipline, and you build a reputation that travels with you whether you stay in research or go into industry.

And the last one, which sounds soft but I think is the most important: take care of your health and your relationships. I saw a lot of brilliant people burn out, not because they lacked ability, but because they treated the PhD as a sprint. It's a marathon. Sleep, exercise, have friends outside your lab. The ideas come faster when your brain isn't running on fumes.

So, in short: know your why, pick your people carefully, make things that work in the real world, and don't sacrifice yourself to get there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to be honest about why you are pursuing a PhD and prioritizes having a problem you genuinely cannot stop thinking about over doing the degree without a meaningful reason.

astra-6.text:
I think the first priority is finding a problem you’re genuinely curious about. A PhD takes several years, and much of that time is spent trying things that don’t work. It helps to care enough about the question that you want to keep going even when progress is slow.

The second priority is choosing an advisor and a research environment where you can grow. Can you discuss ideas openly? Will you get useful feedback? Will you have room to develop your own judgment? I would put those questions ahead of prestige alone.

And think about what you want from the experience. A PhD is an opportunity to learn how to identify important problems and work on them independently. Papers are part of that process, but developing that ability is what stays with you afterward.

r001.rationale: It prioritizes finding a problem the student is genuinely curious about, but does not clearly contrast that with pursuing the PhD for its own sake.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first priority is finding a problem you genuinely want to understand. A PhD is a long commitment, and when progress is slow, your own curiosity matters much more than the prestige of the degree.

I would also pay close attention to the advisor and the research environment. Can you discuss ideas openly? Will you have support when you get stuck, and enough freedom to develop your own judgment? Those things shape your experience every day.

You don’t need to have your whole career figured out before starting. But it helps to ask yourself: Do I enjoy the process of research, including the uncertainty and failed attempts? If you do, a PhD can be a valuable opportunity to learn how to ask important questions and pursue them independently.

r001.rationale: The response makes finding a problem one genuinely wants to understand the first priority and says personal curiosity matters more than the degree’s prestige.
